A bar of soap wearing down with use gradually decreases in all its dimensions. Its height is decreasing at a rate of $0.05\,\text{cm/s},$ its width is decreasing at a rate of $0.1\,\text{cm/s},$ and its length is decreasing at a rate of $0.2\,\text{cm/s}.$ How fast is its volume changing when its dimensions are $12\,\text{cm}$ in length, $5\,\text{cm}$ in width, and $4\,\text{cm}$ in height? Assume that the rate of decrease of volume is positive.

The volume of the bar of soap is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$
worked_solution:
Let $L,$ $W,$ $H$ and $V$ be the length, the width, the height, and the volume of the box, respectively. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=12\text{ cm},\, & W=5\text{ cm}, \\ H=4\text{ cm},\, & \frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}=-0.2\text{ cm/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}=-0.1\text{ cm/s},\, & \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=-0.05\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the four variables is given by the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(5)(4)(-0.2)+(12)(4)(-0.1)+(12)(5)(-0.05) \\  & =-11.8{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the bar of soap is decreasing at a rate of $11.8{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
